lectures.title: What's a Backend? And Why Would You Want One?

cues.en: So for this section,
let's start with the most important question.
What exactly is such a backend and why would we need one?
Well, at this point in the course,
we, of course, built many Flutter apps,
but there's one thing all these Flutter apps had in common.
They, of course, run on the user's device,
their mobile phone.
Therefore, any data that's generated by that app,
like for example, that list of grocery items,
any such data is stored locally on that device.
And therefore, if that device would be lost
or replaced or erased, all the data stored on it
would be lost and erased as well.
Now, for such a shopping list,
that might not really be a problem,
but of course for other kinds of apps,
that might be a huge problem.
Another potential problem is that some apps actually need
to share data with other users.
I mean, the Uber app wouldn't be
that helpful if only you could use it.
Of course, your app must communicate with potential drivers,
and those drivers in the end communicate back to you.
And the same is true for many other apps.
The Amazon app, of course,
would not work if it could only work with data
that's stored locally on your device.
Instead, the Amazon app needs to be able to reach out
to Amazon's servers to load the data from there.
And that's the entire idea
behind adding such a backend server.
The idea is that your app does not need to run
and work alone,
but instead in conjunction with some services and data
provided and stored on such backend servers.
So these servers are really just computers machines running
somewhere in the internet.
And of course, the exact configuration
and which features a certain backend offers
depends on the backend.
Maybe you built it yourselves,
maybe you wrote your own backend logic,
maybe you're using some third party solution.
So that depends.
But in the end, they will very likely
also store data in some database
besides doing other work, which is also possible.
And since they do run in some data centers
somewhere in the internet, of course,
app users from the entire world can interact
with the same data since it's stored in one central place,
instead of on the mobile phones of your users.
Of course, your flutter app must be able to communicate
with those backend servers to use their services and data.
And that communication typically happens via HTTP requests.
And that is exactly what we're going to take a closer look
at in this course section.
We're not going to build a custom backend,
because this course is not about backend development
or using other programming languages.
Instead, we'll use a very simple dummy third party service
as a backend, but you will learn
how you can then send requests to that service
to store data there or retrieve data from there.
And that, of course, will then also allow you to use
that knowledge that you do gain in this section to adapt it
for other use cases where you might be using other backends.

lectures.title: What Is HTTP & How Does It Work?

cues.en: So for certain kinds of apps,
a backend server might be needed.
And as mentioned in the previous lecture,
the communication between your Flutter app
and such a backend server happens via HTTP.
Now, in case you don't really know how HTTP works
or what HTTP requests are, here's a quick overview.
If you do know what HTTP is,
you can of course, skip this lecture.
So HTTP is that thing that in the end allows us
to connect frontend and backend.
It's in the end, a standardized protocol
that's used for communicating back and forth
between a frontend and a backend.
And here's how that works.
It always starts
with the frontend sending a so-called HTTP request
to the backend if it wants something from the backend.
For example, in that shopping list app,
when a new item is added,
you might want to store that on a database
that's managed by the backend,
and therefore you would then send such a HTTP request
from the frontend to the backend, telling the backend
that the data should be stored.
The backend then does its thing,
it does the thing you want it to do,
and then ultimately, it will send back a response.
Though when I say it does the thing you want it to do,
that of course, implies that the backend is prepared
for the kind of work you want it to do.
It's the code on the backend,
the code with which the backend is written
that in the end defines what the backend is able to do
and which kind of HTTP requests it accepts.
In this course section, we're going
to use a dummy third party backend,
a service that offers various backend services.
Alternatively, you could also write your own backend
by using a programming language like Node.js, for example.
That's not what we'll do in this course,

But ultimately, if you send the request
that's supported by the backend to the backend

and did whatever it had to do,
you get back such a response.
And both request and response are in the end,
standardized information packages.
This HTTP thing is a standardized protocol
that in the end defines how requests
and responses may look like.
For example, requests typically contain a URL,
the address of the backend
to which the request should be sent,
an HTTP method that can be picked up by the backend
